note.note:
Consult Summary:
- 35-year-old lawyer reports new-onset, work-associated frontal headaches with mild nausea, intermittent palpitations (often in elevator mornings), shortness of breath at rest (desk) but not with exercise, bilateral hand tingling, reduced appetite, ~5 lb unintentional weight loss, and decreased libido since changing jobs; history of “hyperthyroidism” but takes thyroxine (conflict noted). Plan is for in-person exam and thyroid blood tests.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Severe headaches; triage noted “feeling hot,” but patient did not clearly endorse heat intolerance and instead described intermittent shortness of breath at rest.
- Symptom timeline:
  - Onset: Began around the time of changing jobs (exact date not specified).
  - Pattern: Symptoms occur mostly at work, during meetings or computer use; different symptoms at different times (not all together).
  - Headaches: Frontal, stay localized, often during work (meetings/laptop), intermittently associated with mild nausea. Significantly impacts work.
  - Palpitations: Approximately once daily (sometimes more); sometimes triggered by entering the elevator in the morning.
  - Dyspnea: Occurs while sitting at desk; not present with exercise.
  - Tingling: Bilateral hands/arms; described as quick pricking; no leg involvement.
  - Appetite/weight: Reduced appetite; ~5 lb unintentional weight loss; clothes not notably looser; no external comments on weight loss.
  - Libido: Decreased since job change.
- Exacerbating factors: Work setting (meetings, laptop/sustained reading); elevator exposure for palpitations.
- Relieving factors: Not reported.
- Associated symptoms: Mild nausea with some headaches. No exertional dyspnea.
- Systems review (pertinent negatives/positives as stated): No typical exercise-induced symptoms; no leg tingling. “Feeling hot” not clearly confirmed by patient despite triage note.

Past Medical History:
- Thyroid disease: Patient states “hyperthyroidism,” but is taking thyroxine (levothyroxine), suggesting possible hypothyroidism on replacement vs misstatement (conflict noted).
  - Medication: Thyroxine (levothyroxine) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- No other medical conditions reported.

Social History:
- Occupation: Lawyer in London; approx. 50% meetings and 50% computer/reading; high occupational stress rated 7–8/10.
- Tobacco: Does not smoke.
- Alcohol: “Once a week,” a couple of glasses of wine.
- Recreational drugs: Denies use.
- Other: No additional social factors reported.

Family History:
- Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
- None performed (tele-visit). No vitals documented.

Investigations:
- None completed yet.
- Planned: Thyroid blood tests (“for your thyroxine” per clinician).

Assessment & Plan:
- Issue 1: Recurrent frontal headaches, work-associated
  - Assessment: Likely tension-type/ergonomic and stress-related headaches given localization, work/laptop/reading association, and high stress; mild nausea reported. No focal neurologic deficits reported.
  - Plan:
    - In-person evaluation for full neurologic and general exam.
    - Review workplace ergonomics/posture; encourage regular screen breaks.
    - Defer new medications until after in-person assessment.

- Issue 2: Palpitations and intermittent dyspnea at rest with bilateral hand tingling
  - Assessment: Features consistent with situational anxiety/hyperventilation related to new high-stress job (elevator trigger, desk dyspnea but not with exercise). Thyroid dysfunction (over-replacement or endogenous hyperthyroidism) remains a key alternative/exacerbating factor.
  - Plan:
    - In-person cardiovascular and respiratory exam; consider ECG if palpitations persist or are concerning.
    - Thyroid function tests (TSH, free T4 ± free T3) as planned.
    - Consider brief anxiety screening (e.g., GAD-7) and discussion of stress management and paced-breathing techniques at follow-up.
    - No medications initiated prior to exam.

- Issue 3: Reduced appetite, ~5 lb unintentional weight loss, and decreased libido since job change
  - Assessment: Could be stress-related; thyroid hormone excess is an alternative explanation to assess.
  - Plan:
    - Proceed with thyroid labs as above.
    - Consider basic labs at in-person visit if clinically indicated (e.g., CBC, ferritin, vitamin B12) to evaluate for anemia/nutritional deficiency contributing to paresthesias and systemic symptoms.

- Follow-up/Logistics:
  - Patient to book in-person clinic appointment via app as discussed.
  - No new medications prior to examination and labs.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
- Work-related anxiety/panic with hyperventilation — Likelihood: High
  - Rationale: Onset with new high-stress job; symptoms cluster at work and with triggers (elevator); dyspnea at rest but not with exertion; bilateral hand tingling and palpitations consistent with hyperventilation/anxiety.
- Thyroid dysfunction (possible over-replacement or hyperthyroidism) — Likelihood: Medium
  - Rationale: On thyroxine; weight loss, palpitations, anxiety-like symptoms, decreased libido could reflect excess thyroid hormone. Needs confirmation with labs.
- Tension-type headache (stress/ergonomic) — Likelihood: Medium
  - Rationale: Frontal, non-radiating headaches during meetings/screen time; high stress; minimal migrainous features.

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements: Allergy status not documented; medication dose/route/frequency not documented; exact duration of symptoms not specified; no vitals; no physical exam; family history not provided.
- Conflicts between sources: Patient reports “hyperthyroidism” but is taking thyroxine (typically used for hypothyroidism or replacement) — conflict noted. Triage listed “feeling hot,” but patient did not clearly endorse heat intolerance during interview.
- Transcript quality: Generally understandable; some pauses/unclear segments and brief inaudible portions.
